clean_story: "Repetitive tasks. Machines doing them. The word automation comes from the Greek 'autos,' meaning self, and 'matos,' meaning moving—so, self-moving. A factory line may seem like a dance of human hands, but each bolt tightened, each box sealed, is a task a machine can repeat without pause or error. Automation replaces the rhythm of a worker’s hammer with the precision of a robotic arm, programmed to strike the same spot, at the same force, every time. In a car plant, welding robots fuse metal parts in seconds, where a human might take minutes. At home, a thermostat adjusts temperature before you even notice the chill. These systems follow rules: if this happens, do that. No hesitation. No fatigue. The first industrial robot, Unimate, began assembling cars in 1961, lifting and stacking hot metal pieces with speed no human could match. Three related subjects are robotics, control systems and efficiency in manufacturing."
